items.prompt:
Text A: 'Robins are birds. They have red-orange chests and build nests in trees.'
Text B: 'Robins eat worms. They pull worms out of the ground with their beaks.'

What does Text A tell you about robins that Text B does not?
items.answer: Text A tells us that robins have red-orange chests and build nests in trees. These facts are not in Text B.

steps: Text A: red-orange chests, build nests in trees.
Text B: eat worms, pull them from ground.
Is the nest or chest color mentioned in Text B? No.
Only Text A gives appearance and nesting information.

items.prompt:
Text A: 'Sunflowers turn to face the sun. They can grow very tall.'
Text B: 'Sunflowers have large yellow petals around a dark center. Their seeds can be eaten as a snack.'

What fact appears in BOTH texts?
items.answer: Both texts are about sunflowers. Neither text repeats the same specific fact, but both describe the same plant.

steps: Text A: turn to face the sun, grow tall.
Text B: large yellow petals, dark center, seeds are edible.
Is any specific fact repeated in both? No individual fact is stated in both.
But both texts share the same topic: sunflowers.
The shared element is the topic, not a specific stated fact.

items.prompt:
Text A: 'Polar bears are white. Their fur helps them blend in with the snow and ice.'
Text B: 'Polar bears swim very well. Their large paws help them paddle through icy water.'

Name one thing about polar bears that only Text A discusses and one thing only Text B discusses.
items.answer: Only Text A discusses the white fur and how it helps polar bears blend in with snow. Only Text B discusses swimming and the large paws used for paddling.

steps: Text A only: white fur, blends with snow.
Text B only: swimming, large paws for paddling.
These are separate facts with no overlap.
Each text adds different information about the same animal.

items.prompt:
Text A: 'Bats sleep upside down in dark caves and attics during the day. Their feet can grip surfaces without any effort, so hanging is comfortable.'
Text B: 'Bats hunt at night using a method called echolocation. They send out sounds that bounce off insects, and the echo tells the bat where the insect is.'

Both texts describe bat behavior. How does the behavior in Text A connect to the behavior described in Text B?
items.answer: Text A says bats sleep during the day; Text B says they hunt at night. The two behaviors connect directly: bats rest (Text A) during the day so they are ready to hunt (Text B) at night. The sleeping behavior in Text A supports the hunting behavior in Text B.

steps: Text A: bats sleep during the day in dark places.
Text B: bats hunt at night using echolocation.
How do they connect? Sleeping during the day prepares bats for nighttime hunting.
The resting behavior in Text A enables the activity in Text B.
Both texts show different parts of the same daily cycle.

items.prompt:
Text A: 'Rivers begin high in the mountains where snow melts. They flow downhill to the ocean.'
Text B: 'Rivers provide fresh water for drinking and farming. Many of the world's great cities were built along rivers.'

Text A is about where rivers come from and go. Text B is about how people use rivers. What understanding do you get from both texts together that you would NOT get from either text alone?
items.answer: From Text A alone, you understand rivers as natural features: their origin and path. From Text B alone, you understand rivers as human resources: drinking water and city building. Together, you understand that rivers are both natural systems and essential to human civilization. Neither text alone shows both sides.

steps: Text A alone: natural system (origin in mountains, flows to ocean).
Text B alone: human resource (drinking, farming, cities).
What is missing from each alone?
Text A alone misses how humans depend on rivers.
Text B alone misses what rivers physically are.
Together: rivers are natural water systems AND the foundation of human civilization.

items.prompt:
Text A: 'Camels can go for long periods without water. They store fat in their humps, which their bodies can use for energy when food and water are scarce.'
Text B: 'Cactus plants also survive in the desert with little water. They store water in their thick, fleshy stems and have a waxy coating to prevent water from evaporating.'

Both texts describe desert survival. What strategy do both the camel and the cactus use? How do they differ in how they store what they need?
items.answer: Both the camel and the cactus survive in the desert by storing something inside their bodies. But they differ in what they store: the camel stores fat in its hump (used for energy), while the cactus stores actual water in its stem. The camel stores energy; the cactus stores the water itself.

steps: Camel: stores fat in hump for energy when food and water are scarce.
Cactus: stores water in its thick stem, waxy coating prevents evaporation.
Same strategy: internal storage to survive desert conditions.
Difference: camel stores fat (energy), cactus stores water directly.
Same general approach; different specific resource stored.

items.prompt:
Text A: 'The printing press was invented in the 1400s. It allowed books to be made quickly and cheaply for the first time. Before the printing press, books were copied by hand and very few people owned them.'
Text B: 'The internet allows information to be shared instantly with people all over the world. It has changed how people learn, communicate, and do business in the same way the printing press once changed society.'

Text B directly compares the internet to the printing press. Using specific details from both texts, explain whether this comparison is fair.
items.answer: The comparison is fair. Both technologies dramatically changed how information spreads. Text A shows the printing press made books faster, cheaper, and more available to people who previously had none. Text B shows the internet shares information instantly and globally. Both represent a major leap in information access: from hand-copied books (limited access) to printed books (wider access) to the internet (global instant access). The internet is to our time what the printing press was to the 1400s.

steps: Printing press (Text A): made books fast, cheap, widely available. Before it: hand-copied, rare.
Internet (Text B): information shared instantly worldwide. Changed learning, communication, business.
Comparison: both technologies massively expanded access to information.
Printing press went from rare to common; internet went from slow/local to instant/global.
The comparison is fair because both represent the same type of transformation at different scales.

items.prompt:
Text A: 'Rainforests produce about 20% of the world's oxygen. The trees take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen.'
Text B: 'Every year, large areas of rain forest are cut down for farming and logging. Scientists warn that if deforestation continues, the climate of the entire planet could change.'

Neither text directly says 'we should protect rain forests.' But together, they make that argument. Explain how the two texts build this conclusion without stating it.
items.answer: Text A establishes why rain forests are vital: they produce 20% of the world's oxygen by taking in carbon dioxide. Text B establishes the threat: large areas are cut down each year, and scientists warn this could change the planet's climate. When you combine a thing that is vital (oxygen production) with the fact that it is being destroyed (deforestation), the logical conclusion is that it must be protected. The two texts together build the case without explicitly stating it.

steps: Text A: rain forests produce 20% of Earth's oxygen by absorbing carbon dioxide.
Text B: rain forests are being cut down rapidly; scientists warn of climate change.
What is the logical connection?
If rain forests produce vital oxygen AND they are being destroyed, then destroying them harms oxygen production.
This implies they need protection, even though neither text states it directly.
The argument is built by combining value (Text A) with threat (Text B).
